claim: Telling clinicians to slow down and be reflective does not raise diagnostic accuracy; it only costs time (residents, 20 cases: 44.5% fast vs 45.0% reflective; 69 s vs 89 s per case). Re-checked against the abstract.
agent_test: Add a forced 'be careful and reflect' step to a plain agent and compare to plain at equal tokens; expect no gain.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Cognitive forcing strategy teaching to medical students did not reduce errors on search-satisficing, availability or false-positive cases (n=191; 52% vs 48% searched for a second diagnosis, p=0.91; 45% vs 45% uncommon diagnosis, p=0.98). Re-checked against the abstract. Reviews that call CFS effects 'minor' rest on this and the pilot, so it counts as one source.
agent_test: Give the agent named pitfall rules (search satisficing, availability) in the prompt; test on cases built to trigger each; expect null for a prompt-only rule.

claim: Generic, bias-awareness (debiasing) checklists do not beat a no-checklist control: ECG reading with deliberately bias-inducing cases (n=61), a general debiasing checklist on 5 cases (Shimizu), and a debiasing workshop in clinic (Smith and Slack); in a systematic review cognitive-process checklists helped in 4 of 10 tests.
agent_test: Compare a 'list common biases and check' prompt with plain at equal tokens on bias-injected items; expect no gain.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Checklists that supply content or a task (a differential-diagnosis list, a key-variable list at the verification step, knowledge to retrieve) help more often than bias lists, but the pattern is uneven: the Sibbald 2019 knowledge checklist was null and Chew 2017 helped only on the first half of the test.
agent_test: Add a code-built 'alternatives to consider' list at verify time; measure error corrections per item vs plain at equal tokens.

claim: A checklist used at the verification step, after the first commitment, let experts and residents fix more ECG errors (0.27 vs 0.04 corrected per ECG, n=16; 0.29 vs 0.03, n=15) than a plain silent re-check. Both studies come from one lab.
agent_test: Run the check step as a separate pass with a key-variable list built by code from the case; count corrected vs introduced errors.

claim: Pooled over 29 studies (2732 people), cognitive reasoning tools raise diagnostic accuracy only a little: g=0.20 (0.10-0.29, I2=38%) after removing three studies that trained people first (re-checked in abstract); g=0.28 (0.14-0.43, I2=70%) with them (not in abstract). No moderator found for tool type; the biggest gain was with real or simulated patients (0.41). Other reviews agree gains are small and mixed.
agent_test: Treat any debiasing element as a candidate with an expected small gain; keep only if it wins at equal tokens.

claim: Guided or deliberate reflection helps residents on complex cases but not on simple ones, and not clearly novices; a replication with students (n=186) found no gain on strict scoring (0.47 control vs 0.42 and 0.41), while a dermatology study (n=61) found one (49.7 vs 38.4). Update: LLM analogue seen: extra revision hurt on the easiest medical QA set and wasted tokens on easy math, but helped on harder sets.
agent_test: Apply a reflection or alternatives step only to items the difficulty gate marks hard; compare with applying it to all items.

claim: Reflection during practice can hurt the immediate answer but help a week later (0.48 vs 0.62 immediate; 0.66 vs 0.48 delayed, n=46). The gain is in learning, not in the first answer.
agent_test: Relevant only if the agent keeps memory across items; test whether reflecting on solved items and storing a contrast improves later items.

claim: Raising knowledge of how look-alike diseases differ protected residents from an induced availability bias (0.40 vs 0.24 on biased vignettes, n=91, p=0.004; no effect on unbiased vignettes, 0.36 vs 0.41), where process-only methods had failed. Re-checked against the abstract.
agent_test: Store discriminating features of confusable options in memory and retrieve them at test; compare to a bias warning at equal tokens.

claim: There is little evidence that cognitive debiasing reduces real diagnostic error in practice. Reviews state the evidence is scarce or borrowed from other domains; the share of real errors caused by bias is not established; real-patient interventions with evidence were triggers, review and communication, not debiasing; a clinic debiasing workshop changed little.
agent_test: Do not credit a debiasing step with real-world gain; require a measured gain on our own tasks.

claim: A short web course on pitfalls, mnemonics and Bayesian tools cut errors in mental-health vignettes (n=137, p<.001); this is positive but vignette-only, in a different field, and not replicated here.
agent_test: Not directly testable; use as a boundary note that positive debiasing trials exist.

claim: Process interventions help on hard cases and can hurt on easy ones: the differential checklist raised scores on difficult cases and lowered them on simple ones (Shimizu, re-checked), and reflection improved residents on complex but not simple cases.
agent_test: Run the same alternatives step on easy and hard items; expect harm on easy ones; use the S0 gate to route.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Injected clinical biases lower the accuracy of every LLM tested: BiasMedQA (1,273 USMLE items, 6 models; GPT-4 72.7% without bias, 14.0% worst-case drop under false consensus; GPT-3.5 49.7% with 37.4% average drop), ten-vignette tests (GPT-4 framing, primacy, hindsight), anchoring on 62 forecasting questions, and admissions framing (GPT-4 admits 40.5% more under reject framing). BiasMedQA drops are relative, not points (0.727 to 0.625 is 14.0% relative).
agent_test: Run bias-injected versions of our own items on the plain agent to get a baseline damage figure.

claim: Telling an LLM about the bias (education or awareness prompts) gives small, model-dependent gains: +3.5 to +6.5% across models in BiasMedQA (GPT-4 largest; frequency bias 0.627 to 0.720; none for PMC-Llama), small gains in BiasBuster, and synthetic-clinician prompts left vignette bias mostly unchanged.
agent_test: Compare a one-line bias warning with plain at equal tokens on bias-injected items; check it does not tax plain items.

claim: Example-based debiasing is confounded or fragile: in BiasMedQA GPT-4 no-bias accuracy itself rose from 0.727 to 0.757-0.763 with examples, so gains mix example effect and debiasing; in BiasBuster contrastive and counterfactual examples made models answer always yes or always no.
agent_test: Always report no-bias accuracy of each mitigation arm so example effects are separated.

claim: Prompting an LLM to imitate clinical reasoning styles did not beat plain chain of thought: GPT-4 on MedQA (CoT 76%; differential 78%, p=0.24; analytic 78%; Bayesian 72%, p=0.07); GPT-3.5 was worse (differential 38% vs 46%, p<0.001). Re-checked in the arXiv text; the intuitive-prompt p is 0.9 there, not 0.4.
agent_test: Replicate on our model with a differential-diagnosis prompt vs CoT at equal tokens.

claim: An LLM asked to review its own answer without outside feedback does not improve and often worsens it. GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one round; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0 over two rounds. With oracle stopping GPT-3.5 GSM8K goes 75.9 to 84.3 and GPT-4 95.5 to 97.5. This corrects the evidence lines, which gave 95.5 as the GPT-3.5 oracle score. Update: a 2024 survey finds no success with prompted-LLM feedback outside special tasks, and a 2026 study finds toxic flips as common as real fixes (4.2% vs 5.2% on MATH-500, Qwen3-8B). External or code feedback is what works.
agent_test: Compare an unprompted self-review pass with a signal-triggered revise pass at equal tokens.

claim: A reasoning model (o1) shows less bias than GPT-4 on ten clinical vignette pairs (no measurable bias in 7 of 10; hindsight 52% vs 85%; post hoc 17% vs 56%) but not none, and Occam's razor was fully biased (100% vs 0%). Built-in step-by-step thinking reduces but does not remove bias. Update: an R1 audit (n=100 MedQA, 93%) still found anchoring and too few alternatives; a preprint (not opened) says reasoning does not protect against BiasMedQA biases.
agent_test: Test whether a reasoning-mode setting reduces bias vs a debiasing prompt at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs fail to notice that information is missing or the answer is unavailable, the LLM form of premature closure: models rarely say none-of-the-above (MetaMedQA; unknown recall 0% in 9 of 12 models), pick an answer when the correct option is removed (~70% false action), commit within the first two turns in over 55% of cases, treat more relevant facts as a sign the case is decidable, and stop requesting data in the last round (utilisation 57% to 26%). Most are 2026 preprints not independently re-checked.
agent_test: Add a code-run completeness check (are required fields present) and compare commit rates and accuracy with plain at equal tokens.

claim: Safety or stop prompts reduce but do not remove premature action: false action fell from ~70% to ~48% in one study, and rubric scores rose only 1-3 points on open-ended questions; a hard OLDCARTS completeness gate alone lowered accuracy (38.0% to 32.7%) and helped only when paired with five samples and a semantic-entropy check (49.3%, N=150, one 70B model).
agent_test: Test a code gate on required evidence with and without sample-and-disagree; the gate alone may hurt.

claim: Withholding the diagnostic question until later turns raised first-commit accuracy by up to 62.6%, and models changed wrong answers to right ones up to 10.6 times as often as right to wrong when new evidence arrived. Deferred commitment is a measured lever in staged-evidence tasks.
agent_test: On multi-step items, delay the answer slot until evidence is gathered; compare with immediate answer at equal tokens.

claim: Role-based same-model agents (devil's advocate, facilitator) turned 0/80 correct initial diagnoses into 61/80 (76%) in top-2 after discussion in 16 bias-caused misdiagnosis cases (JMIR version re-checked; an earlier preprint reports 57/80 top-1 and 64/80 top-2 for a different setup); a separate dissent agent cut silent agreement from 61-89% to 11-17% and gave +12.7 points on medical QA. This conflicts with guardrail G9 (no debate); the cases were chosen because the first answer was wrong and there is no no-agent control with matched sampling. Update: three matched-cost reviews (Smit 2024, Wang 2024, Zhang 2025) find debate rarely beats self-consistency or a good single prompt; the one consistent lever is mixing different models. Ke 2024 still has no matched-sampling control.
agent_test: Run the 4-C role setup against five independent samples plus code voting at matched tokens.

claim: Forcing a person to commit or think before AI advice cuts overreliance on wrong AI advice (n=199, six conditions, cognitive forcing functions beat simple explanations; people liked them less; benefit larger for high Need for Cognition; overreliance not removed; paper re-opened), and independent-first judgment reduced misleading-advice acceptance in teachers (OR 1.912, n=218); the second study was seen as a summary only.
agent_test: In an advice-taking setup, have the agent record its own answer before reading the tool or critic output; compare acceptance of wrong advice.

claim: AI-literacy or bias training did not protect physicians from wrong LLM advice (accuracy 73.3% vs 84.9% control, n=44; not opened), and giving physicians GPT-4 access did not raise reasoning scores (76% vs 74%, 95% CI -4 to 8, re-checked), while GPT-4 alone scored 16 points higher.
agent_test: Not directly an agent test; use as caution that human-in-loop does not fix model error.

claim: Wrong cases take longer than right ones (17 s longer; accuracy inversely correlated with time), so time spent is a marker of difficulty or confusion, not a sign of care.
agent_test: Check whether token length per item predicts error on our tasks; use length as a difficulty signal for routing.

claim: Physicians most often name anchoring (60.0%), premature closure (58.5%) and availability (46.2%) as the biases behind their memorable errors (130 forms, Japan); the ED raised the odds of naming a bias 3.96-fold. This is retrospective self-report.
agent_test: Not testable; weak support for picking anchoring and premature closure as the targets.

claim: At matched cost, multi-agent debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or a single strong prompt. MedQA best scores: Medprompt 0.65, debate 0.64, self-consistency 0.60, single 0.60 (GPT-3.5 level). Over 36 configurations debate beat CoT in about 15%; mixing different models helped every debate method (up to +5.8% over CoT-average).
agent_test: Run any role pass (devil's advocate) against an equal-call sampling arm with code voting; add a second model family as its own arm.

claim: Signal-triggered reflection beats always-on reflection: plain self-reflection fixes about as many answers as it breaks (MATH-500 Qwen3-8B: 5.2% effective vs 4.2% toxic), while entropy- or disagreement-triggered reflection gave 3.7% net vs 1.0% and beat budget-matched self-consistency by 3.3-4.8 points (65.2 vs 60.8). Math and commonsense only, one 2026 paper.
agent_test: Fire the check step only when sampled answers disagree or confidence is low; compare with a check on every item at the same token cost on our items.

claim: LLMs show the human 'process helps hard, hurts easy' pattern: sequential revision lowered accuracy on the easiest medical QA task (PubMedQA) and o1-like models spend up to 1,953% more tokens on '2+3' with little gain, while longer reasoning helps on harder sets. Medical evidence is from 7B models; no study splits clinical diagnosis by difficulty.
agent_test: Apply alternatives and reflection steps only to items the difficulty gate marks hard; measure harm on easy items.

claim: Part of LLM clinical bias is self-generated rather than injected: on real oncology notes GPT-4 reasoning errors (23.1% of interpretations, 85.4% reasoning failures) were mainly confirmation and anchoring bias; automated evaluators could not reliably name the subtype. No debiasing step was tested on these.
agent_test: Log trace-level errors on our own items; do not rely on an LLM labeller to type the bias.

claim: Persuasion by a wrong hint grows when the hint comes before the model commits and when it claims expertise: preemptive rebuttals flipped 61.75% vs 56.52% in-context (SycEval, regressive 14.66% overall); 'Thinking' models rationalised expert-labelled wrong nudges; hint harm rose with task difficulty (medical 7B models). No test compares commit-first with advice-first for critic or tool output.
agent_test: Make the commit step precede any critic or tool output and test flip rate of correct answers with a planted wrong critique.

claim: A longer forced think is bounded by knowledge: medical test-time scaling peaks near 4K tokens, 'Wait' forcing adds little without the knowledge, and a reasoning model's errors on MedQA had longer traces. Length can serve as a cheap uncertainty signal.
agent_test: Use trace length or sample disagreement as a gate input; test whether adding discriminating-feature memory beats extra thinking.

claim: Structured fill-in prompts may add a few points on diagnosis quiz cases (60.6% vs 56.5% over zero-shot CoT, p=0.042, snippet only), a size close to the pooled human tool effect (g=0.20). Unverified: full text not opened.
agent_test: Test a code-built category sheet at equal tokens; expect a gain of a few points at most.
